title: Deported Over a Bank's Software, Kamal Budhabhatti Came Back
dek: Sent home to India for a side project, a young clerk borrowed a fare back to Nairobi, lived on his savings and a waived rent, and turned one bank's cheque system into Craft Silicon.

story.event: Returning to Kenya after deportation to finish a bank's cheque-clearing software with no capital
story.summary: Kamal Budhabhatti, a clerk at a Nairobi polythene firm, was deported to India after his employer found him writing software for a friend's bank. He borrowed the fare back from his sister, lived for a year and a half on Ksh23,000 of savings, a waived rent and friends' meals, finished the cheque-clearing system for Ksh200,000 and used it to set up Craft Silicon, whose Bankers Realm software later sold to banks and microfinance institutions in more than 40 countries.
paragraphs: Kamal Budhabhatti came to Kenya from Gujarat, in India, at about 25, and took a job as an accounting clerk at an Indian-owned polythene manufacturer for Ksh18,000 a month. The work was keying invoices into a system. "Every day I used to say I needed to do something better," he later told Forbes Africa. A friend in the house where he lodged was the IT manager of a local bank and wanted a system to automate cheque clearing. Budhabhatti offered to write it in his spare time.

His employer found out. Budhabhatti told How We Made It in Africa that his boss "had me deported back to India"; Forbes Africa reported that the employer drove him home, watched him pack and made sure he boarded the plane. He spent 72 hours at home, then asked his sister to pay for a ticket back. "I felt there was an opportunity here and just had to come back," he said.

What he had on his return was Ksh23,000 in savings, one unfinished job and no other capital. The landlady at his old lodgings let him stay without paying rent, and friends often paid for his meals. The bank, he said, saw that he was desperate, renegotiated the price they had agreed and kept telling him to come back tomorrow. He made the savings last a year and a half, finished the software and was paid Ksh200,000, which he used to settle his debts and set up Craft Silicon.

Smaller banks talked to one another, and he was cheap. Equatorial Commercial Bank, K-Rep and Equity Bank asked for systems of their own, which became the company's first product, a banking platform called Bankers Realm. He later said he took no salary for six years, putting everything into growing the company.

By 2012 Craft Silicon sold its software to banks and microfinance institutions in more than 40 countries, had won the $100,000 grand prize at the 2010 Africa Awards for Entrepreneurship and, by his count, employed about 220 people in Kenya and 100 in India. Asked that year what had made it work, he pointed to time: software, he said, "takes a fairly long time before it starts generating returns."

quote.text: All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small. Therefore the sage, while he never does what is great, is able on that account to accomplish the greatest things.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Laozi's sage reaches great things by never attempting the great thing directly. Budhabhatti did not set out to build a company in 40 countries; he set out to finish one cheque-clearing system for one friend's bank, and stayed with it when it was paid late and paid less.

reflection: It would be easy to tell this as a story of one man's nerve. Look again and it is crowded with other people: a sister who paid a fare, a landlady who waived a rent, friends who bought meals, a bank manager who asked for help. None of them could see Craft Silicon coming. They were helping with something small.

You may be in a small, slow stretch yourself, where the work looks like one job for one person and the money arrives late. Laozi would not call that a failure of ambition. It may be the only place the larger thing can begin, and the people carrying you through it are part of the work, not a debt to be embarrassed about.
invitation: Think of one person who has quietly carried part of your load while you build, as that landlady once did. Send them two lines today saying what their help made possible.

cross_checks.claim: Budhabhatti's employer had him deported to India after discovering he was writing software for a friend's bank
He returned to Kenya, wrote banking software full time and started Craft Silicon without outside capital
By 2012 Craft Silicon served banks and microfinance institutions in more than 40 countries and had won the $100,000 grand prize at the 2010 Africa Awards for Entrepreneurship
Bankers Realm was the company's banking software product

research_notes: Dates: Craft Silicon gives 2000 as its founding year (its Asia team page, as indexed; the bio text is loaded by script and was not visible in the static page), and one low-quality startup directory gives 1998. Forbes Africa (April 2012) says Budhabhatti came to Kenya 'eleven years ago', which would put his arrival around 2001 and, with a year and a half on the bank job, the company somewhat later. The story therefore gives no year for the deportation or founding, and approx_date follows the company's own 2000. A 2017 personal blog (cynthiauntamed.com) dates the finished cheque software to 'around 2007', which conflicts with every other source and was not used. Countries: Forbes Africa (April 2012) and How we made it in Africa's 'Meet the Boss' (May 2012) say 40 and more than 40; the June 2012 interview says 44; the story says more than 40. A 2026 Business Daily interview says 30 markets, apparently counting differently, and is not used. Valuation, not used in the story because the figures disagree widely: Budhabhatti put it at about $30 million in June 2012, while Forbes Africa applied his own multiple-of-20 rule to 2010 turnover of $6 million to reach $120 million. Staff numbers (220 in Kenya, 100 in India) are his own, from one interview, and are attributed. The two How we made it in Africa interviews are from the same publisher, so each cross-check pairs one of them with Forbes Africa or the company site. The Daily Nation's profile ('How I became a billionaire in 10 years') is blocked for the verifier and is not cited. Forbes Africa spells the bank 'KRep'; the story uses its usual name, K-Rep. Quote: Legge's translation of chapter 63; the sage is a model ruler, applied here by analogy to a founder.
